questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman was reviewed in the intensive care with fever and hemodynamic instability. She was recently repatriated to a rehabilitation hospital in the United States from India, where she had been hospitalized for 3 months because of a cerebrovascular accident. She had a peripherally inserted central catheter for blood work, a percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy tube for supplemental alimentation, and an indwelling urinary catheter. Five days earlier, she had developed fever, tachycardia, and hypotension. She was started on meropenem and fluconazole. Investigations: PICC and peripheral blood cultures: positive for Candida haemulonii after 72 hours; susceptibility as follows: Agent Minimum Inhibitory Concentration (MIC) or Mean Effective Concentration (MEC) Interpretation Fluconazole 128 μg/mL Resistant Amphotericin B 2 μg/mL Resistant Micafungin 0.5 μg/mL Susceptible
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely correct identification of the organism?
questions.explanation: Candida auris Candida auris is an emerging multidrug-resistant pathogen that causes otomycosis and invasive candidiasis. It is an important nosocomial pathogen, especially in some parts of the world where it has already established endemicity. Healthcareassociated outbreaks have been reported in the United States. C. auris will be misidentified by commercial identification systems. The Vitek-2 will usually misidentify C. auris as Candida haemulonii and sometimes as Candida famata; the API-20C system will misidentify C. auris as Rhodotorula glutinis, Candida sake, or Saccharomyces cerevisiae. The correct identification can be made through DNA sequencing or with matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization-time of flight (MALDI-TOF).
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q25

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man was seen with a history of intermittent fevers over 6 weeks. He denied any other symptoms. He was being investigated for raised blood sugars and had a dental extraction 7 days earlier. He drank 35 units of alcohol per week. He returned from Malaysia 6 months ago following a 2-month stay with his family during the summer months. On examination, his temperature was 38.9°C, and he had mild abdominal tenderness in his right upper quadrant. Investigations: Total white cell count 17.2 ×109/L CRP 230 mg/L Alanine transaminase 152 U/L Alkaline phosphatase 341 U/L Urgent abdominal USS revealed a single large lesion in the right lobe of the liver consistent with an abscess. No biliary pathology was identified. He was commenced on fluids and IV co-amoxiclav Blood cultures – no growth at 5 days Liver aspirate MCS – mucoid colonies on blood and MacConkey agar. The organism did not react with oxidase or indole A B
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation: Klebsiella pneumoniae K. pneumoniae (K1 capsular serotype) is an emerging pathogen causing liver abscesses in the absence of hepatobiliary disease. It is found in SE Asia, in particular Malaysia. K. pneumoniae are oxidase-negative, lactose fermenting organism. The hypermucoviscous variant grows as very mucoid colonies and can be identified by a positive string test (stretching colonies forms a “string” of >5mm). E. coli is a common causes of liver abscess, and the culture results would fit (although most E. coli are indole positive) but in the absence of hepatobiliary pathology and sterile blood cultures this would be unlikely. E. histolytica commonly presents as an indolent infection and is endemic in rural areas of Malaysia. Against this diagnosis is no preceding colitis (one third) and Entamoeba do not grow on blood or MacConkey agar as they require supplemented media (usually egg yolk). Melioidosis, caused by B. pseudomallei , is a condition causing large abscesses. B. pseudomallei is an environmental saprophyte found in aquatic environments and when cultured grows as mucoid colonies. Going against this as a diagnosis is that infections are most prevalent following the rainy season (rather than summer months when the patient traveled). Also, while it can be found in Malaysia is it more prevalent in Thailand and North Australia. Furthermore, B. pseudomallei are oxidase-positive. Streptococcus intermedius is one of the S. milleri group, which are well recognized as causing deep-seated abscesses such as this. However, the colonial appearances on blood agar are not consistent with S. intermedius, and MacConkey agar does not support its growth. (Image ( left) reprinted with permission from Elsevier. The Lancet. From Prokesch BC, et al. Primary osteomyelitis caused by hypervirulent Klebsiella pneumoniae. Lancet Infect Dis. 2016;16(9):e190–e195. Image ( right) from Rath S, Padhy RN. Prevalence of two multidrug-resistant Klebsiella species in an Indian teaching hospital and adjoining community. J Infect Public Health. 2014;7(6):496–507.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q20

questions.stem: An Escherichia coli isolate is submitted for susceptibility testing. It is resistant to ampicillin, ceftriaxone, and aztreonam, and susceptible to cefoxitin, cefepime, ertapenem, piperacillin/tazobactam, and ciprofloxacin.
questions.lead_in: This pattern is suggestive of drug resistance mediated by what mechanism?
questions.explanation: ESBL Extended-spectrum β-lactamases confer resistance to thirdgeneration cephalosporins but not cephamycins or drugs containing β-lactamase inhibitors.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q45

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman presented with 3 days of diarrhea and severe abdominal pain. She was living in Texas but had traveled to Mexico to visit family 2 weeks prior to presentation. The patient reported drinking raw milk routinely and had a 3-year-old daughter in daycare. Investigations: Multiplex gastrointestinal panel PCR: positive for Shiga toxin 2
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?
questions.explanation: Monitor for development of HUS Although E. coli O157 is the serotype most commonly associated with HUS, any serotype can cause HUS. There is no reason to rule out O157 since the patient should be monitored for HUS regardless of serotype. The presence of Shiga toxin 1 or Shiga toxin 2 is indicative of Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC), not Shigella. If Shigella was present, it would have been detected as Shigella. A Shigella-specific target is part of all currently available GI panels. Antimicrobial treatment of STEC has historically been associated with worse outcomes. There are some newer data that refute this dogma, but the standard practice is still to avoid antimicrobials for STEC.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q1

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man presented in status epilepticus. He was usually fit and well and had returned 1 week earlier from a 2-month visit to Taiwan to visit family. He had no history of recent hospital admission or attendance. He did not take any regular medications, nor did he use any recreational drugs. On examination he had a temperature of 38.3°C, and his pulse was 110 beats/minute. He was sedated, intubated, and transferred to critical care following an urgent CT scan with contrast. Empirical treatment with ceftriaxone and metronidazole was commenced. Investigations: White cell count 23.1 ×109/L (4–11) Neutrophil count 21.8 ×109/L (2–7.5) C-reactive protein 245 mg/L (0–5) Alkaline phosphatase 197 U/L (40–129) ALT 50 U/L (0–41) Total bilirubin 13 μmol/L (0–21) CT head: Liver USS: The liver is heterogenous and mildly enlarged. In the left lobe there is a 79 × 71 × 58mm well-circumscribed, heterogenous area with no vascularity; ? liver abscess
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation: Klebsiella pneumoniae The patient has both cerebral abscesses (ring-enhancing lesions) and a liver abscess. There is a systemic inflammatory response with fever, neutrophilia, and raised C-reactive protein. There is a recognized association of primary liver abscesses caused by Klebsiella pneumoniae with hematogenous spread leading to cerebral abscesses. The travel history should be elicited as there is a higher incidence in SE Asia. (Image from Prayson RA, Neuropathology, 2nd ed. Saunders; 2012.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q3

questions.stem: A patient is admitted with cholangitis and a liver abscess. The abscess was aspirated and cultures grew Enterobacter aerogenes. The isolate was reported to be susceptible to ceftriaxone, and so he was started on that agent. He clinically improved over the next few days but then began to have recurrent fevers, and his liver abscess had reaccumulated when his abdominal imaging was repeated. A percutaneous drain was placed and cultures again grew Enterobacter aerogenes, though now resistant to ceftriaxone.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely mechanism of antibiotic resistance reflected in the different susceptibility profiles?
questions.explanation: AmpC induction Some bacteria, most notably some Enterobacteriaceae, have chromosomally determined ampC β-lactamases that can be expressed at high levels after exposure to β-lactams. This can cause clinical failure even if an isolate initially seems susceptible in vitro.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q42

questions.stem: An 18-year-old man was reviewed with recurrent fevers. He was known to have relapsed acute lymphoblastic leukemia. He had been treated 6 months earlier for a Mediport infection with Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus epidermidis with cefepime and vancomycin. On this admission he was treated with gentamicin and meropenem for an ESBL-producing Escherichia coli bacteremia. Five days after meropenem was started, he spiked a fever to 38.5°C, and another blood culture was drawn. The blood culture signaled positive after 8 hours, and the Gram stain showed gram-negative rods.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely pathogen?
questions.explanation: Stenotrophomonas maltophilia S. maltophilia is one of the few bacteria intrinsically resistant to meropenem. It is also intrinsically resistant to gentamicin. Malignancy and exposure to broad-spectrum antimicrobials, especially carbapenems, are risk factors for S. maltophilia infection. Meropenem is effective against ESBLs and wild-type B. cepacia, M. morganii, and P. aeruginosa. Gentamicin is effective against wild-type B. cepacia, M. morganii, and P. aeruginosa and some ESBLs. While any of those organisms can develop resistance to meropenem, the exposure to meropenem was fairly limited, and acquired meropenem resistance is uncommon in pediatrics.

cohort_answer.text: Residents: Isolate or cohort patients with diarrhea; Contact precautions; Evaluate patients with diarrhea (stool C+S) urgently. Employees: Education/reinforce standard precautions including hand washing; Adherence to contact precautions; Staff with diarrhea should stay home until resolved. Environmental: Disinfect surfaces/rooms often; Private toilet for patients with diarrhea. cohort_answer.text: Organism: Klebsiella pneumoniae with hypermucoviscous phenotype (K1 serotype). questions.question: You are talking with a lab technicians about a Klebsiella isolate which tested resistant to cefazolin, ceftazidime and aztreonam in the lab, but susceptible to cefepime, cefoxitin and meropenem

parts.text: Describe the laboratory method/test to detect the presence of an extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL) in this organism

The lab technician is worried that this could be a metallo-beta-lactamase. Based on the information you have, give 1 reason why a metallo-beta-lactamase is NOT this strain's mechanism of resistance to beta-lactams

cohort_answer.text: ESBL detection: Double disk diffusion comparing a 3rd gen cephalosporin and a 3rd gen cephalosporin + beta lactamase inhibitor; ≥5mm difference is a positive screen for ESBL. (Additional notes: K. pneumoniae/E. coli without carbapenemases typically have imipenem/meropenem MICs <0.5 mcg/mL; overt carbapenem resistance in these species raises suspicion for carbapenemase; certain patterns in other Enterobacteriaceae (e.g. S to 3rd gen cephalosporins, R to imipenem) suggest SMC/NMC/IMI enzymes in Serratia/Enterobacter; P. aeruginosa/A. baumannii can be carbapenem-resistant without a carbapenemase, but Aztreonam susceptibility with high carbapenem/cephalosporin/penicillin resistance suggests an MBL.) Reason MBL is NOT the mechanism here: 1. Meropenem is sensitive. 2. Aztreonam is resistant. (Class B metallo-beta-lactamases are typically R to 3rd gen cephalosporin, S to Aztreonam, R to Cefoxitin, R to Clavulin - the opposite pattern.)

questions.question: Antibiotic susceptibility results become available. A table is given with MICs. The organism is resistant to all beta-lactams except ceftriaxone and ceftazidime (both S) and meropenem (intermediate). It is resistant to ertapenem. You do an imipenem hydrolysis test and find that the organism is a carbapenemase producer.

parts.text: Name the genetic mutation responsible for this resistance pattern.
Name two unique things about this resistance mutation, compared with other carbapenemases.
List 4 other common and clinically relevant carbapenemases that can be found in Enterobacteriaceae.

questions.model_answer:
a) blaOXA-48 (OXA-48-like carbapenemase).
b) Two unique features versus other carbapenemases: (1) OXA-48-like enzymes hydrolyze carbapenems relatively weakly, often producing only modest MIC elevations, so isolates can appear susceptible or intermediate to meropenem/imipenem on routine testing despite being true carbapenemase producers. (2) They have poor/no activity against extended-spectrum cephalosporins, so isolates frequently remain susceptible to ceftriaxone/ceftazidime unless an ESBL is co-produced - unlike KPC or metallo-beta-lactamases, which typically confer broader beta-lactam resistance.
c) Other clinically relevant carbapenemases in Enterobacteriaceae: KPC, NDM, VIM, and IMP.
questions.beyond_mandell: Detailed carbapenemase phenotype comparison is standard clinical microbiology/CLSI knowledge, not covered in this Mandell chapter excerpt.

questions.question: Table of organisms and intrinsic resistance:

parts.text: For Enterobacter, Morganella, and Proteus Mirabilis, indicate intrinsic resistance to Fosfomycin, Nitrofurantoin, Amox/Clav, Cephalexin

questions.model_answer:
Intrinsic resistance pattern (CLSI M100 intrinsic resistance table):
Enterobacter (cloacae complex): intrinsically resistant to amoxicillin-clavulanate and cephalexin (1st-generation cephalosporin) due to inducible chromosomal AmpC; not intrinsically resistant to fosfomycin or nitrofurantoin.
Morganella morganii: intrinsically resistant to amoxicillin-clavulanate, cephalexin, and nitrofurantoin; fosfomycin activity is unreliable/reduced (often considered intrinsically resistant in practice) due to chromosomal AmpC and reduced drug uptake.
Proteus mirabilis: intrinsically resistant to nitrofurantoin (poor urinary concentration/activity against this organism); generally susceptible to fosfomycin, amoxicillin-clavulanate, and cephalexin (lacks a significant inducible AmpC).

questions.question: K. Pneumoniae with resistance to everything, Turns out to be NDM positive

parts.text: What are the two other most common/clinically relevant carbapenemases?
What are two recommended treatments per IDSA guidelines

questions.model_answer:
a) The two other most common/clinically relevant carbapenemases (besides NDM) are KPC and OXA-48-like enzymes.
b) IDSA-recommended treatment options for NDM (metallo-beta-lactamase)-producing organisms: (1) Ceftazidime-avibactam combined with aztreonam (avibactam protects aztreonam from other co-produced beta-lactamases while aztreonam is stable to metallo-beta-lactamase hydrolysis). (2) Cefiderocol monotherapy.

questions.question: Q51 (2023 Day 2). Patient with NDM urinary infection resistant to FQ, TMP-SMX and carbapenems. No other patient details. (UTI)

parts.text: 2 most common carbapenemases
2 first line treatment options in this case as per IDSA

cohort_answer.text:
2 most common carbapenemases: KPC (most common in North America), NDM, OXA-48-like (PHAC data: KPC 48.7%, NDM 28.2%, OXA-48 14.8%).
2 first line treatment options for cystitis caused by CRE: Nitrofurantoin, TMP-SMX, ciprofloxacin, or levofloxacin are preferred (though likelihood of susceptibility is low); alternatives include single dose aminoglycoside, oral fosfomycin (E. coli only), colistin, ceftazidime-avibactam, meropenem-vaborbactam, imipenem-cilastatin-relebactam, cefiderocol. For pyelonephritis/cUTI: TMP-SMX, ciprofloxacin, or levofloxacin preferred if susceptibility demonstrated; ceftazidime-avibactam, meropenem-vaborbactam, imipenem-cilastatin-relebactam, and cefiderocol also preferred; aminoglycosides are alternatives.

questions.question: Per the 2023 IDSA guidelines on the treatment of resistant gram-negative infections, in a critically ill patient with ESBL E coli (non-UTI) with hypoalbuminemia:

parts.text: What is the first line therapy?
Once the patient is clinically improved, name TWO antimicrobials from different classes that are appropriate step down per these same guidelines, provided all the options are susceptible?

questions.model_answer:
a) First-line therapy: a carbapenem - meropenem (or imipenem-cilastatin) is preferred over ertapenem in this critically ill patient, because ertapenem is highly protein-bound and its free (active) drug levels become unpredictable in hypoalbuminemia.
b) Appropriate step-down options (if susceptible), from different classes: a fluoroquinolone (e.g., ciprofloxacin) and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.
questions.beyond_mandell: IDSA 2023 Guidance on the Treatment of Antimicrobial-Resistant Gram-Negative Infections (ESBL-E section).

questions.question: A blood culture bottle returns with Cronobacter sakazakii, formerly Enterobacter sakazakii, and you are consulted on the case.

parts.text: What group/population is at risk for this infection?
What is the source of infection in those who are at risk?
What microbiological feature of this organism assists in its pathogenesis?

questions.model_answer:
a) Neonates and young infants, particularly premature/low-birth-weight infants, are at risk for invasive Cronobacter sakazakii infection (meningitis, sepsis, necrotizing enterocolitis).
b) The source is contaminated reconstituted powdered infant formula.
c) C. sakazakii is notably resistant to desiccation, allowing it to survive for prolonged periods (up to a year) in dry powdered formula, and it expresses outer membrane protein OmpA and a polysaccharide capsule that promote intestinal invasion and crossing of the blood-brain barrier.

questions.question: Q47 (2010 PM). Antibacterial Mechanism of Resistance. Given strain of E coli with the following resistance profile: TMP/SMX (R), Cipro (R), Imi (S), Nitrofurantoin (S), Amp/Cefazolin/Ceftriaxone (R)

parts.text: A) Regarding beta-lactam resistance, two relevant mechanisms of resistance for the above picture?
B) Two confirmatory tests for each mechanism described in (A)

cohort_answer.text: A) Class A beta-lactamase CTX-M (recently described in E. coli, hydrolyzes CRO well, inhibited by PipTazo more than AmoxClav); Class C beta-lactamase AmpC (recently described in E. coli). B) CTX-M: ceftriaxone resistant, cefoxitin susceptible, synergy with clavulin disc on disk diffusion assay. AmpC: ceftriaxone resistant, cefoxitin resistant, no synergy on disk diffusion assay.

questions.question: Q54 (2006 AM). Antibacterial Mechanism of Resistance. A) E. faecium with MIC >256 for both teicoplanin and vancomycin. B) Salmonella enteritidis (resistance stem unclear). C) Enterobacter cloacae resistant to cephalosporins

parts.text: A) Mechanism for E. faecium high-level vanco/teicoplanin resistance
B) Salmonella enteritidis resistance mechanism
C) E. cloacae cephalosporin resistance mechanism

cohort_answer.text: A) VanA gene acquisition - mediates high level vanco resistance by target modification to D-ala-D-lac; most common type, usually higher level resistance, cross-resistance to teicoplanin. B) Incompatible (Inc) plasmids - IncH1 plasmid acquisition leads to concurrent resistance to ampicillin, chloramphenicol, TMP/SMX. C) Class C - AmpC beta-lactamase (chromosomal).

questions.question: Q57 (2003 AM). Antibacterial Mechanism of Resistance. ESBL in Klebsiella pneumoniae

parts.text: a) What is the molecular mechanism of activity?
b) How do you confirm it in the lab?

cohort_answer.text: a) ESBLs are plasmid-based resistance pathways in the accessory genome: TEM beta-lactamases; SHV-1 beta-lactamases (hydrolyze penicillins and narrow-spectrum cephalosporins); CTX-M beta-lactamases (greater activity vs cefotaxime, most common ESBL type worldwide, oxyimino-beta-lactamases hydrolyzing ceftazidime/ceftriaxone/cefepime); OXA beta-lactamases (less common, plasmid-mediated, hydrolyze oxacillin, also in Pseudomonas, confers carbapenemase activity). b) Detection based on resistance to oxyimino-beta-lactam substrates (cefotaxime, ceftazidime, ceftriaxone, cefepime) and ability of beta-lactamase inhibitor (clavulanate) to block resistance; several oxyimino-beta-lactams must be tested; CLSI recommends disk diffusion/broth dilution followed by confirmatory test with clavulanate; other detection: automated systems (Vitek, Microscan), double disk test, E-test strip, pyrosequencing/microarray.

parts.text: A) Name 3 important components of the pathogenesis of HUS?

cohort_answer.text: Disseminates Shiga toxin (stx1 and stx2); Shiga toxins bind GB3 receptors (globotriaosylceramide) found in renal tissue more than any other tissue, also CNS; children have more GB3 receptors hence more susceptible; causes microvascular thrombosis by attacking endothelial cells; kidney is a target; hemolytic anemia (speaker notes: Microangiopathy, thrombosis, hemolysis)

parts.text: B) 3 clinical or lab features

cohort_answer.text: Clinical: Hematuria, Proteinuria, AKI, HTN, Altered LOC, Seizures, prodromal illness of abd pain/vomiting/diarrhea 5-10 days before HUS. Lab: Hemolytic anemia with schistocytes (Coombs negative, low Hb, high LDH); Low platelets; AKI

parts.text: C) 3 risk factors for HUS

cohort_answer.text: <5 years old; Elderly; Antibiotic use (induces expression and release of Shiga toxin); Complement gene mutation; Untreated HIV

parts.text: Name the 3 species from the Enterobacterales family that has the highest risk of clinically important ampC production

For each of the following, indicate if it is a strong or weak inducer of ampC (strong/weak), risk for hydrolysis by ampC (high/low), and if it is recommended for invasive infections (yes/no): Ceftriaxone, Cefepime, Pip-Tazo, Ceftaz-Avi, Imipenem

cohort_answer.text: 3 species: Enterobacter cloacae; Citrobacter freundii; Klebsiella aerogenes. Table - Ceftriaxone: Weak inducer, High hydrolysis risk, Not recommended. Cefepime: Weak inducer, Low hydrolysis risk (MIC<2), Recommended (MIC<4). Tazocin: Weak inducer, High hydrolysis risk, Not recommended. Ceftaz-Avi: Weak inducer, Low hydrolysis risk, Not recommended (limited data, for complicated UTI/intra-abdominal infections only). Imipenem: Strong inducer, Low hydrolysis risk, Recommended

questions.question: Name the most likely mechanism of resistance

parts.text: Serratia marcescens resistant to ertapenem, imipenem AND meropenem, but susceptible to Ceftriaxone
Pseudomonas aeruginosa resistant to Meropenem, but susceptible to Imipenem
Staphylococcus aureus resistant to daptomycin
Enterococcus gallinarum resistant to vancomycin, but susceptible to teicoplanin
Enterobacter cloacae intermediate to ertapenem, but susceptible to meropenem and cefepime

cohort_answer.text: Serratia: Carbapenemase (enzyme inactivation) by SME (oxa-48 also can show this pattern). Pseudomonas: RND efflux pump MexAB-OprM (meropenem/doripenem, but not imipenem, are substrates of this efflux system). S. aureus/dapto: Target-site alteration (change in bacterial cell membrane composition) - dapto requires calcium to become positively charged and interacts with negatively charged lipid moieties on membrane to kill; increased positive charge on membrane prevents dapto action. E. gallinarum: Target-site alteration - VanC (specific to E. gallinarum); vancomycin binds terminal D-ala-D-ala residues of growing PG cell wall; VanA isolates show high MICs to Vancomycin and Teicoplanin, VanB/VanC often have lower MICs to Vancomycin and are S to Teicoplanin. Enterobacter cloacae: Hyperexpression of ampC + porin change combination.

questions.question: Resistance mechanisms for the following:

parts.text: Pseudomonas R to mero and imi; sensitive to piperacillin and ceftaz (give two)
E coli R to cefoxitin, ampicillin but intermediately susceptible to CTX

questions.model_answer: a) Pseudomonas resistant to meropenem/imipenem but susceptible to piperacillin/ceftazidime, two mechanisms: (1) Loss/downregulation of OprD porin channel (carbapenem-specific entry porin) - selectively reduces carbapenem entry without affecting piperacillin/ceftazidime. (2) Carbapenem-hydrolyzing enzyme with narrow spectrum not affecting piperacillin/ceftazidime is less typical; more consistent second mechanism is efflux pump overexpression (e.g. MexAB-OprM) combined with OprD loss - accept efflux pump upregulation as second mechanism. b) E. coli resistant to cefoxitin/ampicillin, intermediate to ceftriaxone (cefotaxime): plasmid-mediated AmpC β-lactamase (e.g. CMY-type) - confers resistance to cephamycins (cefoxitin) and penicillins, with reduced susceptibility extending to third-generation cephalosporins.

questions.question: Question related to antibiotic resistance.

parts.text: Pseudomonas R imipenem and meropenem but S to piperacillin and ceftazidime. Name 2 mechanisms of resistance with molecule/gene (as appropriate)
E coli with R to cefoxitin, amp and cefazolin but I to ceftriaxone. Name one mechanism of resistance with molecule/gene (as appropriate)

questions.model_answer: a) Pseudomonas resistant to imipenem/meropenem, susceptible to piperacillin/ceftazidime - 2 mechanisms with molecule/gene: (1) Loss of OprD porin (oprD gene mutation/downregulation) - selective loss of carbapenem entry. (2) Upregulation of MexAB-OprM efflux pump (mexAB-oprM operon) - effluxes multiple agents but not significantly piperacillin/ceftazidime. b) E. coli resistant to cefoxitin, ampicillin, cefazolin, intermediate to ceftriaxone - mechanism: plasmid-mediated AmpC β-lactamase (e.g. blaCMY gene) conferring cephamycin (cefoxitin) and narrow-spectrum penicillin/cephalosporin resistance with reduced susceptibility to extended-spectrum cephalosporins.

questions.question: Mechanism of Resistance

parts.text: For the following isolates, name the mechanism of resistance: Enterobacter; Pseudomonas R to Imi/Mero, S to Ceftaz; GNB R to mero but increased zone with mero + EDTA; E. coli R to cephalothin but S to cefazolin

cohort_answer.text: Enterobacter - AmpC. Pseudomonas R to Imi/Mero, S to Ceftaz - Porin mediated and efflux pump. GNB R to mero but increased zone with mero+EDTA - Metallo beta lactamase. E. coli R to cephalothin but S to cefazolin - cephalothin breakpoints do not reliably predict susceptibilities of cephalexin and other cephalosporins.

parts.text: Pseudomonas resistant to mero and imi, susceptible to ceftaz, piptaz. 2 resistance mechanisms.
E. coli resistant to ampicillin, cefazolin, cefoxitin (MIC >256), intermediate to ceftriaxone. Mechanism?

questions.model_answer: a) Pseudomonas resistant to meropenem/imipenem, susceptible to ceftazidime/piperacillin-tazobactam - 2 mechanisms: (1) Loss of OprD porin channel (selective carbapenem entry loss). (2) Efflux pump overexpression (MexAB-OprM/MexXY-OprM). b) E. coli resistant to ampicillin, cefazolin, cefoxitin (MIC >256), intermediate to ceftriaxone - mechanism: plasmid-mediated AmpC β-lactamase (e.g. CMY-type) production.

questions.question: Based on the best available evidence, what is the shortest available duration of therapy for the following conditions, assuming clinical improvement and defervesced at 48 hours in each case on therapy?

parts.text: Uncomplicated, fully-susceptible E coli pyelonephritis without any stones or obstruction?
Klebsiella bacteremia due to a now-passed stone with no evidence of abscess or complication?
Fully-susceptible, pulmonary TB without dissemination?
Hospital-acquired S. aureus bacteremia with line removal, repeat blood cultures at 48 hours negative, TEE negative for IE, and no other signs of metastatic infection?
Community acquired pneumonia without microbiologic diagnosis not on oxygen?
Perforated diverticulitis status post OR for washout without any concern of residual abscess per the surgeon?

questions.model_answer: Shortest evidence-based durations: Uncomplicated, fully-susceptible E. coli pyelonephritis (no stones/obstruction) - 5 days (e.g., with a fluoroquinolone); 7 days if using a beta-lactam or TMP-SMX. Klebsiella bacteremia from a passed stone, no abscess/complication - 7 days. Fully-susceptible pulmonary TB without dissemination - 6 months (2 months RIPE + 4 months INH/RIF), the shortest standard regimen. Hospital-acquired S. aureus bacteremia with line removed, negative repeat cultures at 48h, negative TEE, no metastatic infection - 14 days (uncomplicated bacteremia). Community-acquired pneumonia without microbiologic diagnosis, not on oxygen, afebrile by 48h - 5 days (minimum per IDSA/ATS 2019 CAP guideline). Perforated diverticulitis status post operative washout with adequate source control, no residual abscess - 4 days (per fixed-duration antibiotic data, e.g., STOP-IT trial approach).
questions.beyond_mandell: IDSA/ATS CAP guideline (2019), STOP-IT trial (complicated intra-abdominal infection duration), and short-course gram-negative bacteremia trial data (e.g., Yahav et al. 2019) - not covered in this Mandell Staph aureus chapter.

questions.question: Please complete the following table regarding mechanisms of resistance

parts.text: Complete the table (Organism / Antibiotic / Mechanism / Gene associated) for: Enterobacter cloacae (Ceftazidime), MRSA (Daptomycin), Neisseria gonorrhea (Ceftriaxone)

questions.model_answer:
Enterobacter cloacae / Ceftazidime: Mechanism - derepressed hyperproduction of chromosomal AmpC cephalosporinase; Gene - ampC (chromosomal, with regulatory ampR/ampD mutations).
MRSA / Daptomycin: Mechanism - cell membrane remodeling that increases positive surface charge and repels the cationic lipopeptide, plus membrane thickening reducing drug penetration; Gene - mprF (and yycFG/walKR system mutations).
Neisseria gonorrhoeae / Ceftriaxone: Mechanism - altered penicillin-binding protein 2 with reduced cephalosporin affinity, compounded by efflux pump overexpression and porin loss; Gene - penA (mosaic PBP2), with contributions from mtrR and penB.
questions.beyond_mandell: Resistance mechanism/gene detail is general clinical microbiology knowledge, not specific to this Mandell chapter.

questions.question: Q37 (2014). Antibacterial Mechanism of Resistance. What is the mechanism of resistance in the following scenarios: Serratia (Ertapenem R, Imipenem R, Meropenem R, CFTx S); Pseudomonas (Meropenem R, Imipenem S); E. gallinarum (Vancomycin R); E. cloacae (Cefepime S, Meropenem S, Ceftazidime R, Ertapenem R); MRSA (Daptomycin R); MRSA (Linezolid R)

parts.text: State the mechanism of resistance for each scenario

cohort_answer.text: Serratia: Serratia marcescens enzyme (SME) - carbapenemase Class A. Pseudomonas: MexAB-OprM efflux cassette. E. gallinarum: VanC gene presence (chromosomal). E. cloacae: intrinsic resistance to inducible AmpC (R to beta-lactams); OXA-48 (R to Erta, S to Mero with additional efflux pump or porin). MRSA Daptomycin R: mprF gene (phosphatidylglycerol lysyltransferase). MRSA Linezolid R: 23S RNA G2576T point mutation.

cohort_answer.text: Enterobacter - AmpC. Pseudomonas (Imi/Mero R, Ceftaz S) - loss of OprD (porin mutation). GNB (Mero R, increased zone with Mero+EDTA) - metallo-beta-lactamase. E coli (Cephalothin R, Cefazolin S) - beta-lactamase (likely SHV).

questions.question: Q46 (2010 AM, 2009 AM). Antibacterial Mechanism of Resistance (fill in the blank table): K. pneumoniae with Meropenem; P. aeruginosa with Meropenem; E faecium with penicillin; E faecalis with high level aminoglycoside resistance; S. pneumoniae with moxifloxacin; S. pyogenes with erythromycin

parts.text: State the mechanism of resistance for each organism/antibiotic pair

cohort_answer.text: K. pneumoniae/Meropenem: Ambler class D oxacillinases (OXAs); acquired class B beta-lactamases (VIM, NDM); Ambler Class A KPCs; reduced expression of OmpK35/OmpK36. P. aeruginosa/Meropenem: downregulated/absent OprD porin with background AmpC; MBLs (VIM, IMP, SPM-1 less common); upregulation of MexA-MexB-OprM efflux (resistant to mero/doripenem but not imipenem). E. faecium/Penicillin: altered PBPs (resistant pbp5 allele). E. faecalis/HLAR: bifunctional aminoglycoside-modifying enzyme AAC(6')-IE-APH(2'')-Ia. S. pneumoniae/Moxifloxacin: dual mutations in GyrA and ParC. S. pyogenes/Erythromycin: erm gene (ribosome methylation) - methylase enzymes dimethylate adenine on 23S rRNA of 50S subunit, disrupting MLS binding.

questions.question: Q49 (2008). Antibacterial Mechanism of Resistance. Name the resistance mechanism(s) involved: a) Enterobacter - CTZ (R), CTX (R), PipTazo (R), Imipenem (S); b) E coli - Amp (R), Cefazolin (S), Cephalothin (I); c) Pseudomonas - Imi/Mero (R), PipTazo/CTZ (S); d) Pseudomonas - Imipenem (R) MIC=64, MIC with EDTA in agar=0.5

parts.text: State the resistance mechanism for each scenario

cohort_answer.text: a) De-repression of chromosomal AmpC beta-lactamase (class C) in presence of beta-lactams. b) SHV beta-lactamase (class A). c) OprD porin loss (efflux pump would also likely render resistant to tazo/ceftaz). d) Metallo-beta-lactamase (class B).

questions.question: Identify the mechanism: A Pseudomonas isolate is R carbapenems, S PTZ - what is the mechanism of resistance? An E coli isolate is R cefoxitin, S PTZ, S carbapenem, S ceftazidime. What mechanism of resistance?

parts.text: Pseudomonas R carbapenems, S PTZ - mechanism?
E coli R cefoxitin, S PTZ, S carbapenem, S ceftazidime - mechanism?

cohort_answer.text: Pseudomonas: OprD porin mutation (does not cause Piptazo resistance). E. coli: unclear/possibly misremembered stem; discussion suggests possible TEM-1/SHV-1 or AmpC, though the given susceptibility pattern is inconsistent with classic AmpC or ESBL patterns.
